questions.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes
questions.question: Why can plain set-based precision and recall not be computed directly on a ranked retrieval system's output?
options: Ranked systems return too few documents for true positive counts to be statistically meaningful
Relevance judgments become graded rather than binary, which makes true positives ill-defined
A ranker orders the entire corpus, so no retrieved set exists until a cutoff k is chosen
Precision and recall each require a held-out validation split that retrieval systems lack

questions.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes
questions.question: A query has 4 relevant documents; a system places them at ranks 1, 3, 5, and 10. What are P@5 and R@5?

questions.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes
questions.question: You are tuning the first-stage retriever that hands 200 candidates to a reranker. Which offline metric should dominate that stage's evaluation?
options: P@10, because the reranker only reorders whatever already sits in the top ten positions
R@200, because the reranker reorders candidates but cannot recover what the stage missed
P@200, because junk candidates at this depth directly degrade the final ranked page shown
R@10, because users inspect only the first ten results, so deeper recall is wasted work

questions.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes
questions.question: Across your evaluation queries, several queries never exceed P@10 = 0.3 no matter how you tune. What most likely explains this?
options: The reranker keeps discarding relevant documents that the first stage actually retrieved
The queries are too short for the lexical scorer to separate relevant documents from noise
The evaluation depth is set too shallow for recall at that cutoff to ever reach 1.0
Those queries have only about 3 relevant documents, so P@10 cannot exceed roughly 0.3

questions.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes
questions.question: System A places its four relevant hits at ranks 1 through 4; System B places them at ranks 7 through 10. Both score P@10 = 0.4 and R@10 = 1.0. What should you conclude?
options: Cutoff metrics see only top-10 membership, so a rank-sensitive metric must separate them
The two systems genuinely deliver equivalent ranking quality, so either one can ship as is
R@10 was miscomputed, because recall values must differ when hits occupy different positions
P@10 should simply be replaced with P@4, which distinguishes any two rankings that differ

questions.topic: Precision@k and Recall@k: What Ranking Changes
questions.question: Your RAG service always stuffs exactly 5 retrieved chunks into the prompt. Which evaluation choice best matches how the output is consumed?
options: Track R@1000 so that every improvement in the deep candidate pool is fully credited
Track P@10 because it is the community standard cutoff for ranked retrieval evaluation
Track P@5 and R@5, since a relevant chunk ranked sixth never reaches the model at all
Track mean rank of the first relevant chunk, since prompt order determines model attention

questions.question: Which procedure computes average precision for a single query?
options: Average precision at every rank from 1 down to the evaluation depth, then divide by final recall
Average precision at each rank holding a relevant document, dividing by the total relevant count
Multiply precision by recall at the chosen cutoff, then normalize by the count of judged documents
Average the reciprocal ranks of every relevant document retrieved above the evaluation cutoff

questions.question: A query has exactly 2 relevant documents, retrieved at ranks 1 and 4. What is its average precision?
A query has 5 judged relevant documents but your system retrieves only 3 of them within the evaluation depth. How do the 2 missing documents affect AP?
options: They add zero to the sum while still counting in the divisor, dragging AP down
They are excluded from both the sum and the divisor, leaving AP unaffected
They trigger a fallback where AP is computed only over the retrieved subset
They cap AP at exactly 0.5 regardless of where the retrieved three are ranked

questions.question: One query in your set has 40 relevant documents and another has exactly 1. How does MAP weight these two queries?
options: It weights each query by its relevant count, so the 40-document query dominates
It weights each query by retrieval depth, so both contribute in proportion to list length
It weights every query equally, since MAP is a macro-average of per-query AP values
It drops the single-document query, since AP is unstable when few documents are relevant

questions.question: A ranking change lifts MAP by 6%, but every gain comes from relevant documents moving from around rank 40 to rank 20. Your product shows users only 5 results. What is the right read?
options: The lift is real for users, because MAP weights every rank movement by its user impact
The lift proves recall improved, which always translates into better top-5 precision
The lift is spurious, because AP cannot change unless the top 10 positions change
The lift is a product non-event, because MAP credits deep movements users never see

questions.question: Your judges label passages 0 to 3 by usefulness, and you want to report MAP. What does MAP force you to do with those labels first?
options: Rescale them into probabilities so each grade contributes proportionally to precision
Collapse them to relevant versus not at some threshold, discarding the grade distinctions
Average them per document across judges so each passage gets one continuous score
Weight each rank's precision contribution by its grade before averaging over the query

questions.question: Three queries have their first relevant result at ranks 1, 2, and 4. What is the MRR over these queries?
A system returns one relevant document at rank 1 followed by nine irrelevant ones. Under MRR, how does it compare to a system with ten relevant documents in its top 10?
options: The two systems tie, because MRR only inspects the position of the first relevant hit
The second system wins, because MRR sums reciprocal ranks over all relevant hits
The first system wins, because extra relevant documents dilute the reciprocal rank
The comparison is undefined, because MRR requires exactly one relevant document per query

questions.question: Which evaluation pairing best matches the task?
options: MRR for legal-style discovery, where reviewers must eventually find every responsive document
MRR for first-stage candidate generation, where the reranker needs a broad relevant pool
MAP for known-item lookup, where the user wants one specific document as fast as possible
MRR for known-item lookup, where a single correct document satisfies the entire query

questions.question: Under MRR@10, a change moves a query's first relevant hit from rank 10 to rank 11. How does the metric respond?
options: The query's score falls slightly, from 0.10 to about 0.09, matching the small user impact
The query's score falls from 0.10 to 0, an artifact of the cutoff rather than a collapse
The query's score is unchanged, because MRR@10 buckets all ranks beyond 8 together
The query is dropped from the mean, because MRR@10 only averages queries with a hit

questions.question: One query's first relevant hit sits at rank 400 while all others sit in the top 3. Why do practitioners prefer MRR to mean first-relevant rank here?
options: Reciprocal rank is bounded near 0 for deep hits, so one disaster query cannot dominate it
Reciprocal rank grows linearly with depth, so the disaster query is weighted appropriately
Mean rank cannot be computed whenever any query lacks a relevant document in its ranking
Mean rank overweights the easy queries, hiding the single catastrophic query entirely

questions.question: Every query in an evaluation set has exactly one judged relevant passage. You compute both MAP and MRR. What should you expect?
options: MAP exceeds MRR, because AP credits precision at every rank rather than just the first
MRR exceeds MAP, because the reciprocal discount is gentler than the precision dilution
The two diverge only on queries where the relevant passage is ranked first overall
The two are identical, because with one relevant document AP reduces exactly to 1/rank
